column2: Act Ten
The Night Watcher
Night Watch

What a splendid civilization it had been! They had enslaved humanity and built magnificent cities. The ancient records said that the King of Bronze and Fire had lived on the northern ice fields, where he cast a bronze palace as towering as a mountain. There, too, stood the famous bronze pillar that held up the sky, on which the Black King had nailed the White King to death; the enormous column recorded the Black King's long history of war. He had also ordered the construction of a divine road across the ocean, calculated to have been four hundred meters wide—an undertaking greater than any highway today. But when the Black King died, those great monuments vanished, like Atlantis sinking beneath the ocean overnight.

An enormous oak conference table stood amid ranks of bookshelves, surrounded by aged faces. Most of those faces had never appeared on the Cassell College campus. Each was as pale as if it had just been dug out of an ancient tomb. Everyone wore an old-fashioned black tailcoat and an antique-silver ring on the little finger of the left hand.

The younger professors could attend only as standing observers. More than a hundred of them crowded the ground floor of the principal's office. The room formed an atrium open all the way to the roof, where sunlight spilled through the skylight and illuminated Principal Anjou's face at the end of the table.

“Younger professors” meant people like Guderian. Squeezed into a corner, he was trembling with excitement, pinching his bare little finger. Every “young professor” longed for an antique-silver ring, the mark of a tenured lifetime professorship at Cassell. The title generally required more than half a century of teaching at the college. Had these elderly scientists been ordinary humans, they would have developed dementia long ago.

“My God! That's Doug Jones! A landmark figure in the history of nuclear physics! America couldn't have built the atomic bomb without him! The whole world thinks he's dead!” Guderian's voice shook. “And Jean Grus! He's the reason America beat the Soviets to the moon! And he turned down a Nobel Prize! The Americans thought he'd converted to Tibetan Buddhism and retired to Tibet thirty years ago!”
“Aaaah! That's Blair Bittner, the Solomon of mathematics! An Einstein of his field!” Guderian jabbed Manstein with his elbow.
“Stop swooning! I can see pink hearts in your eyes,” Manstein hissed.

“Aren't you excited? You're at a meeting with the milestones of modern science—and they should all be gravestones by now. If the media found out they were alive, the great masters of every discipline would rush here to pay their respects to their teachers' teachers' teachers...” Guderian rubbed his hands. “I hope there's a chance to get their autographs afterward.”
“Wouldn't a photograph be better?”
“My old friend, you're absolutely right! Will you take it for me? Do you think putting my arm around their shoulders would seem too forward?” Guderian punched his palm.
“A souvenir photograph with lunatics? What's the point?” Manstein said coldly.
“Lunatics?” Guderian blinked.

Manstein sighed. “Those so-called milestones in the history of science are sacrifices humanity has offered to the monster called science. Look at them: their skin is pale and withered, but their eyes burn like torches. Some haven't left their laboratories in fifty years. They devote every moment to research, hoping to get a few steps closer to the realm of truth before they die. Their bodies keep declining; only their brains grow stronger. They probably wouldn't mind their limbs withering away until nothing remained but a brain to think with, because thinking is the only meaning in their lives. They're fanatical dreamers of science, lunatics honored with the name of genius. Would you want a life like that?”
“No, not really...” Guderian scratched his head.
Manstein nodded, pleased that his old friend retained a little reason.
“How could I ever deserve to be like them?” Guderian said shyly, like a girl overcome at the sight of her idol. “I'd be content to serve tea and water to those madmen racing toward the truth...”
Manstein silently covered his face, unable to describe his sense of helplessness.
“Quiet,” Anjou said softly.

The two took the hint and shut up. In fact, they had been the only ones whispering since entering the room. The other “young professors” wore expressions as solemn as if their parents had died, while the “lifetime professors,” occasionally let out of their academic sanctuaries for air, showed no expression at all—like the dead parents themselves.

“Everyone is here. Let's begin. Blair, my old friend, it's been half a century. It's a pleasure to see you alive in person.” Anjou glanced at the “Solomon.” “And to my other old friends, our distinguished department heads, it's a pleasure to see you face to face. I'm sorry to interrupt your research, but we had compelling reasons. The report has been sent to you all; I trust you've read it.”
Everyone with a seat at the table was a department head at Cassell College. Most students knew only which department they belonged to; they had no idea the heads even existed.

“From the standpoint of physics, humans cannot yet do it,” said Doug Jones, head of physics, in a low voice. His back was hunched, his aging spine bent almost into a circle, and he coughed as he spoke. He looked as if a missed breath would suffocate him.

He operated the touchpad on the table, projecting two black-and-white photographs in midair: the ruins of South Railway Station and of the Midgard Serpent. The twisted aluminum girders and rails had a grotesque beauty, like the bones of snakes stripped of flesh and wrenched out of shape.

“Both structures collapsed because of stresses within them—ghostlike stresses that, once unleashed, easily destroyed metal structures built to withstand a magnitude-nine earthquake.” Doug Jones shook his head. “If humans knew how to trigger such stress, a poke of a finger could destroy the entire Hoover Dam.”
“Ghostlike stress?” The “young professors” exchanged looks. Even coming from a scholar at the pinnacle of his field, the claim was extraordinary.

“We examined the Midgard Serpent's blueprints. It is one of only three roller coasters of its class in the world. Because no one had designed a coaster that demanding before, every place that called for one-inch steel was enlarged to five inches for safety. Even an F-22 fighter crashing head-on into it might not bring it down,” said Jean Grus, head of precision mechanics. “Yet stress destroyed it. That silent stress was more astonishing than the kinetic energy of an F-22 cruising at supersonic speed. That's why we call it ghostlike.”

Blair Bittner frowned. “Grus, the young people are weak on mechanics. Explain the basic concept of stress first!” The Solomon of mathematics certainly lived up to his reputation. Both hands resting on an ivory-trimmed black cane, he sat bolt upright in a hardwood chair, his hair a lion's raging mane. He looked rather like a Japanese samurai preparing to disembowel himself, his face radiating regal authority.
The “young professors,” whose average age was fifty, all looked ashamed.

“Simply put, when a force acts on an entire metal structure, the resisting force within that structure is stress. If the force is torsion, the resisting force is shear stress. Shear stress forms a flow: enormous forces move through the metal like water, with a particularly high concentration at weak and narrow points. Once that concentration passes a threshold, the structure begins to fail,” Jean Grus said.
“Then shear stress should be the enemy of every building. Why was it so destructive in these two?” someone asked.

“Good question. As we said, shear stress flows through metal parts like water, but not evenly; it resembles chaotic turbulence. Small flows cancel one another out and never grow unmanageable. There are exceptions, however.” The Solomon glanced at Grus. “Mechanic, this is your field.”

Grus nodded. “Yes. We call that exception stress concentration. In an instant, flows of shear stress happen to converge on a vulnerable joint, producing an enormous resultant force that destroys it. But to guide that concentration, or awaken the ghostlike stress, one must analyze the complete structure of the building. The computation is terrifying; even Norma can't do it. That's why we say it lies beyond human ability.” He looked around. “Does anyone know the ancient martial arts of the East?”
The room fell silent.
Grus nodded. “Lately I've been studying a Chinese martial art called the Vajra One-Finger Zen.”

The room remained silent. The minds of academic geniuses were truly like dragons whose heads appeared while their tails remained hidden. Everyone else was lost in a fog, unsure what he meant. Only the Solomon nodded slightly, apparently a fellow lover of martial arts.

Grus raised a thick, short finger, his eyes shining. “Vajra One-Finger Zen is a Shaolin art. It is said that a master can shatter a stone tablet with one finger. That fascinated me. A finger bone consists of water, protein, and a little calcium; it is actually fragile, easily broken with a light twist. How could it act like a high-hardness alloy drill bit? Yet there is evidence that people really mastered this ancient art. After six months of research with my colleagues, thousands of repeated experiments, and several colleagues breaking their index fingers, we finally found the secret. It lies in where and how you strike. The most exquisite force must hit the most vulnerable point. The Chinese call it the ‘eye’ or an ‘acupoint.’ Rock has its eye, and steel has its eye. Pour force through that eye like running water and guide the ghostlike stress. The resulting concentration fractures the entire target, even reducing it to powder in an instant.”

“So,” Anjou said, “the enemy who ambushed us at South Railway Station and Six Flags is a mysterious old martial artist whose control of force has reached perfection. If he wished, he could destroy the Capitol or the Pentagon with a single blow?”
“So it was an old martial artist,” Guderian said thoughtfully.
“An old martial artist might break a stone tablet, but the Midgard Serpent was built from high-strength steel,” Manstein said quietly. “Their ‘old martial artist’ is something else...”
“One of the Four Monarchs... the King of Earth and Mountain!” the Solomon said softly.

Dead silence settled over the room. The ancient title had stunned everyone. Though they had long known of this Dragon King from old books, and though he now appeared in their minds in the comical guise of an elderly Eastern martial artist, no one could laugh. It was as if a vast black shadow had fallen over them, heavy as a mountain.

“He is the master of the earth, and the element he commands is earth. No dragon in the world is more skilled at controlling force. The records say, ‘The waves of stone herald his stretching before he wakes. The day he stretches to his full extent, mountains become abysses.’ He can even break through the earth's crust,” Anjou said softly.
“If he's awake, why hasn't he appeared before us directly? With his control of force, none of us could resist. We would be at his mercy,” someone asked.

“I don't know.” Anjou shook his head. “Perhaps something still gives him pause. Perhaps the one awakened this time is not the Dragon King himself but one of his descendants, a noble second-generation dragon. Whatever the case, a new dragon must have awakened behind these two incidents. Every dragon is our enemy. Given the chance, he will grind every one of us into dust! Rather than wait helplessly, we must sharpen our blades. This time we face an awakened dragon whose father may be the great Black King Nidhogg himself. This is a meeting to prepare for war. When it ends, the highest-level dragon-threat alert will go out across the world. A new war is about to begin.”

The lifetime professors rose one after another. With the “young professors,” they placed hands over their hearts and spoke solemnly: “Good shall triumph over evil. Wherever light reaches, darkness has nowhere to hide.”

After seeing the lifetime professors off, Anjou returned to his desk on the third floor. A bone-china teapot and two cups stood on it; the Darjeeling inside was still warm. A listless young man sat beside the desk. The lifetime professors who had met downstairs had never imagined a student was listening in, much less that he had a seat and tea and refreshments, when even Manstein, head of the Discipline Committee, had to stand.
“Mingfei, won't you try a scone? They're hazelnut.” Anjou sat opposite him, lit a cigar, and picked up his tea.
“I'm not in the mood...” Lu Mingfei sighed. “Principal, is it okay for me to listen in on a meeting like that? You know I have a big mouth sometimes. What if I let something slip?”

“The meeting happened to fall during the principal's afternoon tea, and you're the student I invited today. I'm sorry it interrupted our pleasant tea break; I merely asked you to wait here.” Anjou shrugged.
“But everything you talked about was classified.”
“I have something even more confidential. Would you like to hear it?”

Lu Mingfei covered his ears. “Forget it. Even if I can keep my mouth shut, what if I talk in my sleep? Anyway, it has nothing to do with me... Principal, if a Dragon King really is awake, I won't be on the dragon-slaying strike team again, will I? I already risked my life going to a Dragon King's house. That kind of thing uses up your luck... I think I need at least a hundred years to build it up before I go again!”

“I'm afraid there's no help for it. It's time to reveal some secrets to you. As our only S-rank student, there are things you'll have to learn sooner or later.” Anjou set down his cup and gently pressed a red button hidden in the drawer.
Lu Mingfei felt his chair and the entire floor tremble. Then he, Anjou, the huge nanmu desk, and the steaming tea on it all sank into boundless darkness together.
“Ah! Is it an earthquake? An earthquake?” Lu Mingfei shouted.
“No. We're descending.” Anjou's cigar tip glowed and dimmed in the dark.
“Descending?” Lu Mingfei blinked. “Where to?”
“The other half of Cassell College.”

The floor and desk jolted again, gradually slowed, and stopped sinking. Light suddenly appeared on every side. Lu Mingfei looked up and saw a shark! And not just the enormous hammerhead: a languid sea turtle floated to his left, a bluefin tuna over two meters long swam to his right, and great schools of mackerel raced around him. Everywhere he looked, rippling water cast shifting light and shadows.
“This is our aquarium,” Anjou explained. “We're in the underwater passage beneath it.”
“An... aquarium?” Lu Mingfei was bewildered. “How did we get into an aquarium?”
“Strictly speaking, we're in an elevator. A VIP elevator reserved for the principal.”
“An elevator?” Lu Mingfei was even more confused.
“The floor is the size of this platform, with transparent glass walls around it. That's my elevator,” Anjou said. “It just sank into the underwater passage.”

“What kind of VIP elevator has room for a whole desk? Isn't that a little extravagant?” Lu Mingfei murmured. Anjou's desk alone was larger than an ordinary elevator car—and when they descended, his liquor cabinet had come down too!
“Would a man who harbors the great dream of saving the world care about spending such a trifling sum?” the old man protested weakly.

The “elevator” suddenly moved, not up or down but sideways. It slid through the encircling school of mackerel. The hammerhead and sea turtle paid the moving glass room little attention; presumably they were used to it.

“The aquarium houses all kinds of marine life. It's the college's genetic repository. Research on dragons requires a large number of genetic samples for comparison,” Anjou explained. “The aquarium is only part of this underground space, of course. We're going to see the rest. For the next little while, you'll be visiting the most highly classified area of Cassell College. It's also known as the Ice Cellar.”

“The Ice Cellar?” Lu Mingfei wondered if he had heard wrong. Few students were allowed in. Legend said Cassell kept alchemical equipment and dangerous weapons there, and those who had been inside never spoke of it.

“You all think the Ice Cellar is merely a storeroom or a display room? That's only one part of it. Ice Cellar is the collective name for the college's underground buildings, which are far larger than the campus aboveground. You've never seen those department heads, have you? At an ordinary college it would be unthinkable for department heads never to appear on campus, but at Cassell their real work is research, and all their laboratories are underground. Norma's mainframe is here too, as well as heavy research equipment and even a subway train leading outside!” Anjou said proudly. “This underground space combines electronic, mechanical, and alchemical technology. No human can break in.”
“So... a dragon could?”
Anjou paused, a little embarrassed. “No dragon has broken in either, but we have found mice down here... We don't know how they got in.”
“That's not secure at all!”
“Ahead is our botanical garden,” Anjou said.

A lush green expanse appeared beneath Lu Mingfei's feet, but it was no lawn or flower garden. It was a forest! Two elevated rails swept over the treetops, and their “elevator” was crossing a subtropical forest. There was even sunlight overhead!

“Artificial sunlight, providing energy for photosynthesis. This is a huge fissure in the earth. The space isn't really that large, but it holds more than 120,000 species of plants,” Anjou said. “There's a zoo next door with more than 8,000 species, from pigs to pandas, but it has never been open to visitors.”
The elevator entered the heart of the “mountain” through a cleft in the rock, then soon emerged again.
“What's that? It looks like a pyramid!” Lu Mingfei cried, pointing ahead.

“Oh, it is a pyramid.” The old man answered casually. “We pulled it out of a South American jungle, transported it here, and reconstructed it. Quite an undertaking. We chartered a seventy-thousand-ton container ship and marked every stone so we wouldn't put it back together incorrectly.”
The principal's elevator stopped in front of the pyramid, and they followed a metal stairway onto the enormous concrete base supporting it.

“Notice anything different about it?” Anjou led Lu Mingfei around the pyramid. It was built entirely of black stone blocks without any binding agent, like a construction of toy blocks. Its stability depended on its own weight and precise cutting. Though somewhat worn, the surface carvings remained clear. Its builders had carved patterns into the hard black stone and filled the deep grooves with molten copper.
“It seems... to have an extra face?” Lu Mingfei said.

“Correct. Unlike every other pyramid, it has five sides, each with 133 stone steps. Every step is covered in ancient Mayan characters—numbers, to be precise. The entire pyramid is a Mayan calendar, the whole history of the world as the Maya saw it.” Anjou stroked the black stone. “But what the Maya called history was not only the past... it was also the future.”
Lu Mingfei stared.
“It is a book of the past, the present, and the future. It is a history book and a book of prophecy.”
“That's too deep.” Lu Mingfei scratched his head.
“Have you seen 2012?”
“Yes.” Lu Mingfei nodded. “The story where a science-fiction writer saves his ex-wife when the world ends.”
“The director borrowed the date 2012 from the Mayan calendar. It is the most important date in that calendar: the year the Fifth Sun ends.”
Lu Mingfei nodded, only half understanding.

“The Maya were remarkable. They were the most precise astronomical observers of antiquity, even able to observe the far side of the moon, which never faces Earth. They created the solar calendar: a calendar, a history, and a book of prophecy. They wrote the future into history because they believed it was already determined. The history of this world is finite; it need not extend forever. There are five Suns. Advanced civilizations existed in the first four, but each ended in destruction: Matlactli was destroyed by flood, Ehecatl by wind serpents, Quiahuitl by a rain of fire, and Tzontlilic by upheavals of the earth. Fortunately, each previous catastrophe spared an ancient civilization, and that civilization began a new Sun. But there will be no sixth. After the Fifth Sun, there is nothing: zero, emptiness, the destruction of all things.” Anjou said, “Neither dragons nor humans will survive that end.”
Lu Mingfei suddenly remembered something and shivered involuntarily. “Wait, wait. Those four earlier destructions... flood, wind serpents, fire rain... upheaval of the earth...”
“Yes. Earth, water, wind, and fire. They are represented by the Four Monarchs on the dragon thrones. Each of the first four destructions was caused by one monarch. No one knows about the fifth.”
“The Black King?” Lu Mingfei felt cold sweat breaking out.

“The Maya didn't say. Perhaps the Black King, perhaps the White King, perhaps all Four Monarchs together. You enrolled in 2009. If we can't deal with this catastrophe, I don't think you'll get your diploma.” Anjou shrugged.

“Hey, that's heresy, isn't it? Why should we believe the Maya?” Lu Mingfei came to his senses. “They were just primitive people, right? If they were so amazing, how did they get wiped out? Who did it? Spaniards with guns and cannons?”

“Ancient Mayan civilization declined in the eighth century. As their states broke apart, their priests lost their traditions. Before the Spaniards arrived, they had already lost the ancient calendar and all their mystical knowledge.” Anjou spread his hands. “But that doesn't mean their prophecies are unreliable. One could say that none of history's books of prophecy were written by humans... Humans merely passed them on.”
“Dragons?”
Anjou nodded. “This is something the dragons left behind.”

“Wait. Principal, you said neither humans nor dragons can survive the Fifth Sun, and the dragons made the Mayan calendar. Doesn't that mean... the dragons predicted their own extinction?” Lu Mingfei asked.

“Yes. Dragon prophecies are prophecies of destruction, because in their view, destruction is the world's inevitable end. Norse mythology was most deeply influenced by dragon culture. The poets who recorded it did not describe enticing futures like reincarnation or heaven; they described death directly. Ragnarok is the destined day of destruction, when giants and the dead will attack the realm of the gods. Therefore Odin built Valhalla and ordered the Valkyries to bring the souls of brave warriors there. Day after day they practice fighting, drink, battle one another, die, and rise again, preparing to take the field at the end. Even so, the outcome cannot be changed. The myths record clearly how the gods will end, who will kill whom, with no exception even for Odin. Norse mythology moves in one direction, with no cycle and no branching paths, like the thread spun on the loom of the three goddesses of fate: straight ahead, all the way to... death! That is also the dragons' view of the world. Every Dragon King has foreseen his end, yet they keep cocooning themselves and awakening, trying to resist.”
“That sounds so sad,” Lu Mingfei said softly.
“It's our view of the world too.”
“Then it's not just sad; it's downright miserable...” Lu Mingfei pulled a face.
“Destruction is a recurring theme in myths around the world. Some put it more gently than the Norse did, that's all,” Anjou said. “Have you read Journey to the West?”
“Even a cheerful book like that has something to do with doomsday?” Lu Mingfei's eyes widened.

“In Journey to the West, Patriarch Subhuti tells Sun Wukong that practitioners of the Way fear the ‘three terrible calamities’: three fated trials, which are in fact the three disasters of Buddhist mythology. The Shurangama Sutra describes them. First comes fire: seven suns appear in the sky at once and burn the world, destroying everything from Avici Hell to the first dhyana heaven of the form realm. Then comes water, flooding everything from Avici Hell to the second dhyana heaven. The third is wind, scattering all matter from Avici Hell to the third dhyana heaven.” Anjou glanced at Lu Mingfei. “You see the connection?”
“It's a lot like the Mayan myths,” Lu Mingfei said. “Earth, water, wind, fire.”

“Yes. There's also the great flood mentioned in many mythologies. People living tens of thousands of miles apart in the East and West all believed a flood once destroyed the world. The Chinese tell of Yu the Great controlling the waters; the Bible says God told Noah to build an ark of gopher wood to escape the flood. The earliest record is a Sumerian clay tablet from 3500 BC. Scholars still debate it, but a great deal of evidence shows that a flood once covered most of the earth and cut a break through human history,” Anjou said. “Dragon prophecies of destruction have been confirmed again and again. But none of us knows what will happen in 2012. We've been waiting, wondering what might happen... and then it really did. The long-silent Dragon Kings are awakening one after another, a collective awakening unprecedented in history. Mingfei, do you know what you should do now?”

“No! You've scared me half to death, Principal! Have you built a big ship in the Himalayas? Are tickets on sale?” Lu Mingfei's face was blank. He truly didn't know what expression suited a conversation like this. His life had scarcely begun to be good, and it seemed it was already about to end.

“Cassell College is a Valhalla. A hundred years ago we began assembling an army of the finest dragon-blooded descendants. We don't know what we'll face, but this army must be strong enough to adapt to any battlefield.” Anjou patted Lu Mingfei's shoulder. “And you're one of its finest.”

“I'm one of its finest? I have to say, Principal, your plan for the end of the world sounds shaky! Say aliens invade Earth, and the president makes a stirring speech, then appoints Nobita Nobi commander in chief of the entire army—Nobita without Doraemon! What if we fail? What if the world is destroyed? Building a big ship sounds more reliable!”

“This is the big ship.” Anjou gestured around them. “There are five underground spaces like this in the world, some deep in mines, others beneath glaciers. Each natural space has been excavated and stocked with vast numbers of plants and animals, as well as embryos, pollen, and seeds. All of human civilization has been preserved, along with knowledge of alchemy and Yanling. There are complete sets of machinery, and of course food and drinking water. Deep in the Ice Cellar is a miniature reactor with enough energy to run this place for five hundred years. If you fail, I'll retire here.”
“That sounds like a Nationalist commander frightened by the Communist charge, firing a few shots into the air and hiding straight in a shelter...” Lu Mingfei covered his face.

“Some people must go to battle, and some must live on.” Anjou leaned against the railing beside the concrete base, the wind lifting his white hair. “I might be the one who dies, and you the one who retires.”
“Now that sounds a little more loyal!”

“Remember my friend Meinhard?” Anjou said softly. “When we first founded the Lionheart Society together, he often drank with me and said that if we faced a Dragon King one day, the last man standing should run as quickly as he could. ‘Someone has to carry on the soul of our Lionheart Society, doesn't he?’ he always said. ‘So who should survive? Well, I'd quite like to live myself, but I think Anjou would be better. Women like him, and genetically speaking, men women like have better genes. He's got the potential to be a playboy, have countless children with countless beautiful women, and train them all as new members of the Lionheart Society. Ha ha ha ha!’” Anjou imitated the man's laughter, gazing up at the sky lit by artificial light. “In the end, he really did die, and I survived.”

“When I first went to Cambridge, I was on a scholarship and had very little money. Whenever I had any, I had nice clothes made to catch the girls' attention, and often went hungry. Meinhard was my senior then, and he always invited me to eat at his place. He was good at cooking foie gras and often made it himself. I'd drink red wine and watch him bustle around. I'd say, ‘Meinhard, you're wonderful,’ and he'd say, ‘You don't need to thank me. Someday you can cook for your junior. If your junior cooks for his junior too, that would really be wonderful... Ha ha ha ha.’” Anjou smiled. “You have no idea how much he loved to laugh.”
“I was joking just now.” He turned to Lu Mingfei. “I won't retire here. I've already lived alone as the last man once. That was enough.”
Lu Mingfei was silent for a long time. Looking up, he saw a black iron case being carried along the suspended track into the depths. “Do we really have a chance?”
“I don't know.” Anjou shrugged. “Remember what I told you in Chicago? That is all I have, and for it I'll pay any price.”

He glanced at the black iron case overhead. “The remains of the Dragon King Constantine, the only dragonbone cross in the world we can currently confirm. It was in the alchemy laboratory for analysis, but we had to move it to the deepest level and bury it. Too many people are interested in it.”

Chu Zihang slowly opened his eyes. Everything before him was pure white and blurred. He believed in neither God nor heaven, but the face bending over him was unadorned and flawless, suffused with warm light, like an angel lowering her head to kiss a sinner's forehead.
For an instant he was dazed. He tried to lean closer to see her face clearly. He smelled the angel's warm, moist scent, carrying the fragrance of leaves after rain.
“Senior, are you getting fresh with me the moment you wake up?” she said leisurely, just as he was about to bring his whole face close.

“Xia Mi?” Chu Zihang's vision gradually cleared. He lay in an intensive care ward, sunlight passing through white curtains. Tubes and wires ran all over his body, and doctors and nurses came and went.
“That's right! Not an angel, just your junior, because you aren't dead.” Xia Mi seemed to read his mind.

“Not dead?” Chu Zihang tried to move his limbs. Aside from an ache everywhere, every bone was intact. It was incredible. When he lost consciousness and fell, he'd been at the highest point of the track, with no air cushion below. However much he strengthened his bloodline, the body was still supported by human bones made chiefly of calcium carbonate. He couldn't fall two hundred meters and emerge unscathed.

“Does your body hurt? High-voltage current went through you and made your muscles spasm and go numb. Rest and you'll recover. You were lucky: if the current had passed through your heart, an angel really would be welcoming you now.” Xia Mi rested her chin in her hand and tilted her head. “This is the college's intensive care ward. You've been unconscious for ten days, kept alive on intravenous nutrients.”
“So... I didn't die,” Chu Zihang said softly.
“You sound disappointed.” Xia Mi rolled her eyes. “Come on, Senior, you escaped death! Could you stop being so expressionless and look happy?”
Chu Zihang stared for a moment, then pulled up the corners of his mouth in a silent smile.
“Not sincere at all!” Xia Mi pouted. “You should say thank you! You survived because your junior was incredibly brave and rushed up to catch you!”

Chu Zihang pressed a hand to his forehead. His memories were confused, but in the long, long dream before he woke he had dimly felt someone holding him, a faint scent of plants at his nose, letting him sleep on in peace.
“I used my Yanling, Wind King's Eye,” Xia Mi said.
Chu Zihang nodded. “So your Yanling is Wind King's Eye. No wonder you weren't afraid on the roller coaster.”

Yanling: Wind King's Eye, sequence number seventy-four. Within its domain, centered on the user, it manipulates airflow to form a vortex. With sufficient control, the user can hover in the air and even move through it briefly.

“Nothing of the sort. I was scared to death; I was just too embarrassed to say so. Do you think Wind King's Eye works like wings? Changing the path of a fall by manipulating air is easy enough, but landing safely depends on luck. We fell into the deep water on the rapids ride.” Xia Mi huffed. “You make it sound so easy, but I took a huge risk! If I could really fly, why wouldn't I fly to America instead of paying for a plane ticket?”
Chu Zihang couldn't be bothered to argue with her nonsense. He was tired, his eyelids heavy, so he closed his eyes.
“Saving you gives me no sense of accomplishment.” Xia Mi sounded a little angry.
“Why?”
“I've never seen anyone who values his own life so little! If you think your life is worthless, why should I risk mine to save you?” Xia Mi said indignantly.
“I don't want to die.” Chu Zihang kept his eyes closed. “I just couldn't think of another way.”
“Do you like cosplaying a hero that much?”

“No. Once before, someone died behind me, and I did nothing. I just kept driving forward... By the time I realized I was a coward and wanted desperately to go back for him, I couldn't find him anymore.” Chu Zihang spoke softly. “Do you understand that feeling? If you still have a life to risk, don't wait until you regret it before risking it.”
“What feeling?”
“The feeling of ‘I'm a coward.’” Chu Zihang opened his eyes and looked at the ceiling.

The Night Watcher nodded. “You're an undertaker, so you always wear black and carry a folding knife in your sleeve. For a hundred years, every moment you've thought of killing—no, slaying dragons. You're the sort who holds a grudge. Anyone who makes an enemy of you has only death waiting, unless they kill you first. I just wonder why you're so stubborn.”
“And what are you thinking? Why have you stayed at Cassell all these years? Don't tell me you're here drinking beer in retirement.” Anjou turned to look at him.
The Night Watcher scratched his head. “I'm not telling you... I don't want to make up a lie.”
Anjou laughed. “You, honest? You used to sweet-talk women all the time.”
“But you aren't a woman, so I can't lie to you.”
“You're like a man who'd die if he couldn't make a bad joke.” Anjou picked up the umbrella he'd brought and headed for the door. He had achieved his purpose in coming.
“Hey, Anjou,” the Night Watcher said behind him.
Anjou stopped, neither speaking nor turning around.

“I don't like the tycoons and politicians on the board. For their interests they can sacrifice anyone. Politicians have no morals or limits to begin with. But they still want to build: to create a new age of hybrids and hold power in it. You only want to bury the dragons... I believe you. Given the chance, you'll end them with the mushroom clouds of nuclear bombs. When fire rains from the sky, you'll light a cigar and pour a glass of champagne to honor your old friends. Your life is spent waiting for that moment of performance art,” the Night Watcher said quietly. “But Anjou, think carefully. All you want is destruction. You care about nothing else. You've reached a dead end. Who do you think you are? The goddess of vengeance?”
Anjou stood in the doorway beneath his umbrella, rain falling from its edge. He gazed at the iron-gray sky, apparently thinking, his back blurred and distant.
“You're wrong,” Anjou said gravely. “The god of vengeance.”
